Checkpoint: independent binding with finite supplies

Set qR1=qR2=qG=1 μMq_{R_1}=q_{R_2}=q_G=1\,\mu\mathrm M, K1=K2=1 μMK_1=K_2=1\,\mu\mathrm M and ω=1\omega=1. Compare the either-bound fraction with the value obtained by substituting totals for free inputs.

Worked answer

Independence factors the occupancies, so each balance reads 1=R+R/(1+R)1=R+R/(1+R) in micromolar units. The positive root is R=(5−1)/2≈0.618 μMR=(\sqrt5-1)/2\approx0.618\,\mu\mathrm M. The either-bound fraction is 1−(1+R)−2≈0.6181-(1+R)^{-2}\approx0.618, while substituting totals gives 0.75. Independent binding does not remove finite-pool depletion.

Derive combined regulation from joint states and their activities, test mechanisms along the diagonal where isolated curves agree, and close the regulator totals whenever their supplies are finite.

22At low copy number the state is a distribution

At small copy numbers the equilibrium object is a probability distribution over molecule counts, not a concentration. The core's note on promoters in §12 relies on two facts about that distribution, and this section proves both.

The first fact is an identity for occupancy. Let m labelled sites be exchangeable, and let c count the occupied ones. With IiI_i the indicator that site i is occupied, c=∑iIic=\sum_iI_i, and linearity of expectation gives

Pr⁡(Ii=1)=E[c]m.\Pr(I_i=1)=\frac{\mathbb E[c]}{m}.

The identity needs exchangeability, not independence. A finite ligand supply can correlate the sites while keeping their marginal probabilities equal.

The second fact is that the distribution is exact and small. Take nEn_E enzyme molecules, nSn_S substrate molecules and c complexes in a volume V. The association and dissociation propensities are k+S(nE−c)(nS−c)/(NAV)k_{+S}(n_E-c)(n_S-c)/(N_AV) and k−Sck_{-S}c, where NAN_A converts moles to molecules. Define nKd=KdNAVn_{K_d}=K_dN_AV, the dissociation constant counted in molecules. Detailed balance gives

π(c+1)π(c)=(nE−c)(nS−c)nKd(c+1),π(c)∝(nE)c (nS)cc! nKdc,\frac{\pi(c+1)}{\pi(c)}=\frac{(n_E-c)(n_S-c)}{n_{K_d}(c+1)},\qquad \pi(c)\propto\frac{(n_E)_c\,(n_S)_c}{c!\,n_{K_d}^c},

where π is the stationary distribution, (n)c=n(n−1)⋯(n−c+1)(n)_c=n(n-1)\cdots(n-c+1) is the falling factorial, and 0≤c≤min⁡(nE,nS)0\le c\le\min(n_E,n_S).

A two-enzyme example shows the distinction. With nE=2n_E=2, nS=1n_S=1 and nKd=0.1n_{K_d}=0.1, the complex is present with probability 20/2120/21, and each enzyme is occupied with probability 10/2110/21. Both enzymes are never occupied together, because only one substrate exists. The deterministic root of the same numbers gives 0.916 complexes, while the stochastic mean is 0.952. The concentration model is a macroscopic description, and averages at low counts must use the distribution.

A promoter in maintained regulator reservoirs is the case where the two agree. There the normalized weights of §21 are the probabilities of the discrete promoter states, and their activity-weighted sum is the mean production rate. Lecture 6's fast-switching limit justifies using that mean for slow dynamics. A finite regulator pool needs the conditional distribution at the relevant counts instead.

Use the exchangeability identity for mean occupancy, the exact count distribution for any low-copy average, and the concentration model only where reservoirs make the two coincide.

23The open enzyme closes the dynamics

The core's coda closes a binding-catalysis model with supply and removal on the same totals. This section does it for the reversible enzyme of §9, derives the steady state exactly, and runs the pipeline on a supply sweep.

1 · Model. Order the species as x=(E,S,P,CES,CEP)x=(E,S,P,C_{ES},C_{EP}). The substrate and product bind the enzyme, and catalysis is one resolved reversible chemical step:

E+S⇌k−Sk+SCES⇌kcat−kcat+CEP⇌k+Pk−PE+P.E+S\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-S}]{k_{+S}}C_{ES}\xrightleftharpoons[k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{-}]{k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}}C_{EP}\xrightleftharpoons[k_{+P}]{k_{-P}}E+P.

Supply and export are composite boundary processes, ∅⇝S\varnothing\rightsquigarrow S and P⇝∅P\rightsquigarrow\varnothing, with rate laws vinv_{\mathrm{in}} and vout=koutPv_{\mathrm{out}}=k_{\mathrm{out}}P. Only free product is exported.

The accumulation line follows from the species equations. Let vbS=k+SES−k−SCESv_{\mathrm{b}S}=k_{+S}ES-k_{-S}C_{ES} and vbP=k+PEP−k−PCEPv_{\mathrm{b}P}=k_{+P}EP-k_{-P}C_{EP} be the net binding fluxes, and v+−v−=kcat+CES−kcat−CEPv_+-v_-=k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}C_{ES}-k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{-}C_{EP} the net catalytic flux. Then

E˙=−vbS−vbP,S˙=vin−vbS,P˙=−vbP−koutP,C˙ES=vbS−(v+−v−),C˙EP=vbP+(v+−v−).\begin{aligned}\dot E&=-v_{\mathrm{b}S}-v_{\mathrm{b}P},&\dot S&=v_{\mathrm{in}}-v_{\mathrm{b}S},&\dot P&=-v_{\mathrm{b}P}-k_{\mathrm{out}}P,\\\dot C_{ES}&=v_{\mathrm{b}S}-(v_+-v_-),&\dot C_{EP}&=v_{\mathrm{b}P}+(v_+-v_-).&&\end{aligned}

Adding rows with the counts of L cancels every binding flux. The enzyme total qE=E+CES+CEPq_E=E+C_{ES}+C_{EP} is constant, and the two form totals qS=S+CESq_S=S+C_{ES} and qP=P+CEPq_P=P+C_{EP} obey

q˙S=vin−(v+−v−),q˙P=(v+−v−)−koutP.\dot q_S=v_{\mathrm{in}}-(v_+-v_-),\qquad \dot q_P=(v_+-v_-)-k_{\mathrm{out}}P.

This is q˙=S v+Sextvext\dot q=S\,v+S^{\mathrm{ext}}v^{\mathrm{ext}} with the matrices of §9, where the external fluxes form their own stoichiometric term.5 Catalysis changes the two form totals, yet each is conserved by binding, so both are slow coordinates.

The binding layer solves by one scalar equation. With Kd,SCES=ESK_{d,S}C_{ES}=ES and Kd,PCEP=EPK_{d,P}C_{EP}=EP, eliminating each ligand with its form total gives

CES=qSEKd,S+E,CEP=qPEKd,P+E,E+qSEKd,S+E+qPEKd,P+E=qE.C_{ES}=\frac{q_SE}{K_{d,S}+E},\qquad C_{EP}=\frac{q_PE}{K_{d,P}+E},\qquad E+\frac{q_SE}{K_{d,S}+E}+\frac{q_PE}{K_{d,P}+E}=q_E.

The last equation is monotone in E on (0,qE)(0,q_E). At each integration step it supplies the states that catalysis and selective export read.

2 · Experiment. Vary the supply vinv_{\mathrm{in}} and read the steady state. At steady state v+−v−=vin=koutPv_+-v_-=v_{\mathrm{in}}=k_{\mathrm{out}}P, so the supply fixes P=vin/koutP=v_{\mathrm{in}}/k_{\mathrm{out}} and the form totals become outputs. The binding relation gives CEP=EP/Kd,PC_{EP}=EP/K_{d,P}, and the catalytic balance gives CES=vin/kcat++(kcat−/kcat+) CEPC_{ES}=v_{\mathrm{in}}/k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}+(k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{-}/k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+})\,C_{EP}. The enzyme total then yields the exact steady state:

E=qE−vin/kcat+1+(1+kcat−/kcat+) vin/(koutKd,P),S=Kd,S CESE.E=\frac{q_E-v_{\mathrm{in}}/k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}}{1+\bigl(1+k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{-}/k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}\bigr)\,v_{\mathrm{in}}/(k_{\mathrm{out}}K_{d,P})},\qquad S=\frac{K_{d,S}\,C_{ES}}{E}.

Every concentration is positive when 0<vin<kcat+qE0<v_{\mathrm{in}}<k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}q_E. The upper limit is the capacity. At or above it the reduced model has no finite steady substrate inventory. The illustrative values are qE=Kd,S=Kd,P=1 μMq_E=K_{d,S}=K_{d,P}=1\,\mu\mathrm M, kcat+=1 s−1k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}=1\,\mathrm s^{-1}, kcat−=0.2 s−1k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{-}=0.2\,\mathrm s^{-1} and kout=0.3 s−1k_{\mathrm{out}}=0.3\,\mathrm s^{-1}.

3 · Candidates. The enzyme total is at most either affinity, so CES/S=E/Kd,S<1C_{ES}/S=E/K_{d,S}<1 and CEP/P=E/Kd,P<1C_{EP}/P=E/K_{d,P}<1. Free S and free P win their form totals at every supply. Only the enzyme total can change winner, among E, CESC_{ES} and CEPC_{EP}.

4 · Regime sequence. At low supply the path is in (E,S,P)(E,S,P), with E≈qEE\approx q_E. The ratio CEP/E=P/Kd,P=vin/(koutKd,P)C_{EP}/E=P/K_{d,P}=v_{\mathrm{in}}/(k_{\mathrm{out}}K_{d,P}) is exact, so the check CEP<EC_{EP}<E fails at vin=koutKd,P=0.3v_{\mathrm{in}}=k_{\mathrm{out}}K_{d,P}=0.3. The check CES<EC_{ES}<E would fail later, at 0.6. The walk therefore predicts a product-bound regime (CEP,S,P)(C_{EP},S,P) next. Its checks hold for koutKd,P<vin<(kcat+−kcat−)qEk_{\mathrm{out}}K_{d,P}<v_{\mathrm{in}}<(k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}-k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{-})q_E, which is 0.3 to 0.8. Near capacity the path is in (CES,S,P)(C_{ES},S,P).

The exact curve overrules the middle prediction. The exact winners are E below vin=0.278v_{\mathrm{in}}=0.278, the root of 10v2+8v−3=010v^2+8v-3=0, and CESC_{ES} above it. At the crossing E=CES=0.342E=C_{ES}=0.342 and CEP=0.317C_{EP}=0.317, the closest that CEPC_{EP} ever comes to winning. The predicted band is only a factor 2.7 wide, and its checks pass by margins under two. This is the warning case of §15. All three candidates stay within a factor of two of one another, so leading order names a winner that the exact solve does not confirm. A real product-inhibition regime needs koutKd,P≪(kcat+−kcat−)qEk_{\mathrm{out}}K_{d,P}\ll(k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}-k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{-})q_E, through slow export or tight product binding.

5 · Response. The substrate inventory is the readout. In (E,S,P)(E,S,P), S≈Kd,SCES/qES\approx K_{d,S}C_{ES}/q_E with CES≈vin(1+kcat−qE/(koutKd,P))/kcat+C_{ES}\approx v_{\mathrm{in}}(1+k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{-}q_E/(k_{\mathrm{out}}K_{d,P}))/k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}. Near capacity, the exact E is proportional to the capacity gap qE−vin/kcat+q_E-v_{\mathrm{in}}/k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{+}, and S is inversely proportional to it.

Supply, export and enzyme capacity

Change supply or export and compare the substrate and product inventories required for steady operation.

Both binding scales are 1 µM. Forward and reverse catalytic rates are 1 and 0.2 s⁻¹. Only free product is exported.

Close a binding-catalysis model by deriving the accumulation of each form total, solve its steady state exactly, and read the regimes of the enzyme total along the supply, trusting leading order only where its checks pass by a wide margin.

24Test a reduction on the output it must predict

A reduction is tested by comparing it with the resolved dynamics on the output of interest. The test keeps the equilibrium constants fixed and speeds up binding, so that only the clock separation changes.

The protocol has four parts. First, set k+S=k+P=ε−1 μM−1s−1k_{+S}=k_{+P}=\varepsilon^{-1}\,\mu\mathrm M^{-1}\mathrm s^{-1}, and choose k−Sk_{-S} and k−Pk_{-P} to keep Kd,SK_{d,S} and Kd,PK_{d,P} fixed. The catalytic and export rates are unchanged, so ε measures binding speed against the fixed catalytic clock. Second, start the resolved and reduced models at the same state, the reduced steady state at supply 0.2 μM s−10.2\,\mu\mathrm M\,\mathrm s^{-1}, and step the supply to 0.4 at time zero. Third, compare the two form totals on 301 samples over 60 s, and record the largest absolute error in either. Fourth, control the numerics. The stiff resolved equations use an implicit Radau method with relative tolerance 2×10−102\times10^{-10} and absolute tolerance 2×10−12 μM2\times10^{-12}\,\mu\mathrm M. The reduced system is integrated independently by DOP853 and by fixed-step RK4, which agree to within 10−9 μM10^{-9}\,\mu\mathrm M. The resolved enzyme total stays constant to numerical precision.

The error falls in proportion to ε across the tested range. The control speeds up only substrate binding and leaves product binding on its original clock. The fully equilibrated reduction then keeps a total error near 3.21 μM3.21\,\mu\mathrm M, however fast substrate binding becomes. A valid partial reduction would keep product binding dynamic rather than eliminate it.

Test a reduction against resolved dynamics with its equilibrium held fixed, and measure the error on the totals or outputs the model must predict.

25Gains enter the slow Jacobian

The gains of Part 3 are the binding layer's contribution to slow dynamics. The Jacobian of the closed model factors into stoichiometry, flux size, pool size and these gains, and each factor can be read separately.

Start with the log sensitivities of the activities. For a positive activity vα=∑jkαjxjv_\alpha=\sum_jk_{\alpha j}x_j with nonnegative coefficients, define Fαi=∂log⁡vα/∂log⁡qiF_{\alpha i}=\partial\log v_\alpha/\partial\log q_i. The chain rule through the gain matrix H=∂log⁡x/∂log⁡qH=\partial\log x/\partial\log q of §7 gives

Fαi=∑jkαjxjvα Hji,Dqv=diag⁡(v) F diag⁡(q)−1.F_{\alpha i}=\sum_j\frac{k_{\alpha j}x_j}{v_\alpha}\,H_{ji},\qquad D_qv=\operatorname{diag}(v)\,F\,\operatorname{diag}(q)^{-1}.

The weights kαjxj/vαk_{\alpha j}x_j/v_\alpha are the shares of the activity carried by each state, and they sum to one. So the sensitivity of a process is the share-weighted average of its states' gains. At leading order one state carries the activity, and its row of LTL⋆−1L^{\mathsf T}L_\star^{-1} becomes the process's sensitivity (§11).

The Jacobian of the slow model follows. For q˙=S v+Sextvext\dot q=S\,v+S^{\mathrm{ext}}v^{\mathrm{ext}}, with S=LΓcatS=L\Gamma_{\mathrm{cat}},

Jq=S diag⁡(v) F diag⁡(q)−1+Dq(Sextvext).J_q=S\,\operatorname{diag}(v)\,F\,\operatorname{diag}(q)^{-1}+D_q\bigl(S^{\mathrm{ext}}v^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigr).

Stoichiometry enters through S, flux size through diag⁡(v)\operatorname{diag}(v), pool size through diag⁡(q)−1\operatorname{diag}(q)^{-1}, and binding through F. Within a regime F is a matrix of rational gains, so the Jacobian inherits the regime's structure. Lecture 9 uses this structure for stability, and Lecture 11 develops the geometry of the possible gains.

Directional activities must stay separate. Write v+v_+ and v−v_- as two positive activities before taking logarithms. A net flux can vanish at equilibrium or at a stall, where its logarithm is undefined. The derivative of the net flux is still finite, as the difference of two well-defined terms. Keeping the two directions preserves the physics near balance and avoids spurious infinite sensitivities.

Build the slow Jacobian from stoichiometry, fluxes, pools and binding gains, keeping forward and reverse activities as separate positive terms.

Optional · further runs of the pipeline

The pipeline on further mechanisms

Core A1 to A3 run the pipeline three more times. This part derives those runs and adds four mechanisms the core leaves out: negative cooperativity, hidden conformations, series binding and a modification cycle. It ends with the pipeline stated for a system that no lecture has met.

26The winner of the repressor total sets the Hill degree

Core A1 shows that a dimerizing repressor gives a Hill law of degree two in total repressor only in one regime. This section derives the exact inventory, the exact midpoint and the table, with exact values beside the laws.

1 · Model. Two free repressor monomers R bind as the dimer CRRC_{RR}, and the dimer binds the promoter G as CGRRC_{GRR}:

2R⇌k−dimk+dimCRR,G+CRR⇌k−promk+promCGRR.2R\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-\mathrm{dim}}]{k_{+\mathrm{dim}}}C_{RR},\qquad G+C_{RR}\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-\mathrm{prom}}]{k_{+\mathrm{prom}}}C_{GRR}.

The dimer association flux is defined as k+dimR2k_{+\mathrm{dim}}R^2, so any combinatorial factor sits inside that rate constant. The dissociation constants are Kdim=k−dim/k+dimK_{\mathrm{dim}}=k_{-\mathrm{dim}}/k_{+\mathrm{dim}} and Kprom=k−prom/k+promK_{\mathrm{prom}}=k_{-\mathrm{prom}}/k_{+\mathrm{prom}}, both concentrations. Only free G produces, through the composite process G⇝G+XG\rightsquigarrow G+X with rate law v=k0Gv=k_0G. The binding relations and totals are

CRR=R2Kdim,CGRR=G CRRKprom,qG=G+CGRR,qR=R+2CRR+2CGRR.C_{RR}=\frac{R^2}{K_{\mathrm{dim}}},\qquad C_{GRR}=\frac{G\,C_{RR}}{K_{\mathrm{prom}}},\qquad q_G=G+C_{GRR},\qquad q_R=R+2C_{RR}+2C_{GRR}.

The promoter total eliminates G, and the repressor total becomes one scalar equation for free monomer:

GqG=11+R2/KH2,qR=R+2R2Kdim+2qGR2KH2+R2,KH=KdimKprom.\frac{G}{q_G}=\frac{1}{1+R^2/K_H^2},\qquad q_R=R+\frac{2R^2}{K_{\mathrm{dim}}}+\frac{2q_GR^2}{K_H^2+R^2},\qquad K_H=\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{dim}}K_{\mathrm{prom}}}.

The right side of the second equation increases from zero to infinity with R, so every repressor total has one root. The solve keeps both dimer storage and promoter loading.

2 · Experiment. Sweep the repressor total qRq_R, and read the free promoter fraction G/qGG/q_G.

3 · Candidates. The promoter is in trace, 2qG≪qR2q_G\ll q_R, so CGRRC_{GRR} never wins the repressor total (§15). The repressor total has candidates R and 2CRR2C_{RR}, which tie at R=Kdim/2R=K_{\mathrm{dim}}/2. The promoter total has candidates G and CGRRC_{GRR}, which tie at R=KHR=K_H. A regime is named by the winners of (qR,qG)(q_R,q_G).

4 · Regime sequence. The order of the two ties decides the sequence. When KH<Kdim/2K_H<K_{\mathrm{dim}}/2, the promoter switches while the monomer still wins, and the path runs through (R,G)(R,G), (R,CGRR)(R,C_{GRR}) and (CRR,CGRR)(C_{RR},C_{GRR}). When KH>Kdim/2K_H>K_{\mathrm{dim}}/2, the dimer takes the repressor total first, and the path runs through (R,G)(R,G), (CRR,G)(C_{RR},G) and (CRR,CGRR)(C_{RR},C_{GRR}). Every crossing is regular.

5 · Response. Where the monomer wins, R≈qRR\approx q_R. Where the dimer wins, CRR≈qR/2C_{RR}\approx q_R/2, and the binding relation gives R≈(KdimqR/2)1/2R\approx(K_{\mathrm{dim}}q_R/2)^{1/2}. The monomer's gain drops from 1 to 1/2 at that crossing, a rational change (§15). The exact column uses the two panels of Figure 20, both with KH=1 μMK_H=1\,\mu\mathrm M and qG=10−4 μMq_G=10^{-4}\,\mu\mathrm M.

The exact midpoint tests which regime a measured curve is in. At half activity R=KHR=K_H, so CRR=KpromC_{RR}=K_{\mathrm{prom}} and CGRR=qG/2C_{GRR}=q_G/2. The repressor total there is

qR,1/2=KH+2Kprom+qG.q_{R,1/2}=K_H+2K_{\mathrm{prom}}+q_G.

The three terms count free monomer, free-dimer constituents and promoter-bound constituents at the midpoint. A Hill-2 law in total repressor needs the first term to exceed both others. In the left panel the terms are 1, 0.02 and 0.0001, so the midpoint is 1.0201 μM1.0201\,\mu\mathrm M and the monomer wins. In the right panel they are 1, 200 and 0.0001, so the dimer wins, and the midpoint sits at 2Kprom2K_{\mathrm{prom}}.

Self-repression closes this model, and the closure needs a removal law. Let the product X be the repressor itself, so production is G⇝G+RG\rightsquigarrow G+R. The repressor total then obeys q˙R=k0G−vout\dot q_R=k_0G-v_{\mathrm{out}}, where voutv_{\mathrm{out}} must say which protein states are removed. Removing every form at one frequency δR\delta_R gives vout=δRqRv_{\mathrm{out}}=\delta_Rq_R. Removing only free monomer gives vout=δRRv_{\mathrm{out}}=\delta_RR. The two choices give different slow dynamics from the same equilibrium.

Count every protein copy, find the winner of the repressor total, and only then assign a Hill degree to a response plotted against total protein.

27A sponge moves the threshold

Core A2 shows that a tight sponge moves a promoter's threshold to the sponge total. This section derives the exact inventory, runs the pipeline twice, and then shows that the same stored material slows the free signal.

1 · Model. Free repressor R binds the promoter G or the sponge T:

G+R⇌k−Gk+GCGR,T+R⇌k−Tk+TCRT,KGR=GRCGR,KRT=RTCRT.G+R\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-G}]{k_{+G}}C_{GR},\qquad T+R\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-T}]{k_{+T}}C_{RT},\qquad K_{GR}=\frac{GR}{C_{GR}},\qquad K_{RT}=\frac{RT}{C_{RT}}.

qR=R+qGRKGR+R+qTRKRT+R,GqG=KGRKGR+R.q_R=R+\frac{q_GR}{K_{GR}+R}+\frac{q_TR}{K_{RT}+R},\qquad \frac{G}{q_G}=\frac{K_{GR}}{K_{GR}+R}.

qR,1/2=KGR+qG2+qTKGRKRT+KGR.q_{R,1/2}=K_{GR}+\frac{q_G}{2}+\frac{q_TK_{GR}}{K_{RT}+K_{GR}}.

Run 2: a tight promoter makes a rectifier

3 · Candidates. A tight promoter changes this step, because the promoter total is no longer in trace. The complex CGRC_{GR} now becomes a candidate of the repressor total. Take KRT≪KGR≪qGK_{RT}\ll K_{GR}\ll q_G, so the sponge binds first and the promoter binds next. The illustrative values are KGR=0.001K_{GR}=0.001, KRT=10−5K_{RT}=10^{-5}, qG=1q_G=1 and qT=2 μMq_T=2\,\mu\mathrm M.

qR−qT=R+CGR−T.q_R-q_T=R+C_{GR}-T.

Its candidates are walked like any others. While the promoter has room, CGRC_{GR} carries the balance, so G≈qG−(qR−qT)G\approx q_G-(q_R-q_T). Once the promoter is full, free repressor carries it, R≈qR−qT−qGR\approx q_R-q_T-q_G, and G≈KGRqG/RG\approx K_{GR}q_G/R.

A sponge also slows the free signal

The stored material that moves the threshold also buffers changes in free R. Take supply and removal as composite processes, ∅⇝R\varnothing\rightsquigarrow R with rate law u and R⇝∅R\rightsquigarrow\varnothing with rate law δRR\delta_RR, so only free repressor is removed. The total obeys q˙R=u−δRR\dot q_R=u-\delta_RR. Differentiating the equilibrium inventory in R gives

dqRdR=β(R)=1+qGKGR(KGR+R)2+qTKRT(KRT+R)2,R˙=u−δRRβ(R).\frac{dq_R}{dR}=\beta(R)=1+\frac{q_GK_{GR}}{(K_{GR}+R)^2}+\frac{q_TK_{RT}}{(K_{RT}+R)^2},\qquad \dot R=\frac{u-\delta_RR}{\beta(R)}.

Here β is the buffering factor, the change in total repressor per unit change in free repressor. Because β≥1\beta\ge1, loading slows every change in free R. Near a steady state the relaxation time is β(R∗)/δR\beta(R^*)/\delta_R, where R∗=u/δRR^*=u/\delta_R is the steady free repressor. The steady free level does not depend on the sponge at fixed supply. The total and the transient do. At fixed total, by contrast, adding a sponge lowers free R directly. Retroactivity theory makes exactly this distinction between a module in isolation and a module under load.15

Increase the sponge amount and see how much total repressor is needed to repress the same gene.

Gene total 0.1 µM; gene–repressor dissociation scale 1 µM. Both complexes count toward total repressor.

Solve static sequestration and dynamic buffering from one shared inventory, and use the ray's balance to place the threshold and to test any shifted law.

Core A3 shows that one inactive extra state turns a rising response into a window. This section derives the window's exact peak and then runs the pipeline on a conformational ensemble, the MWC model.

Checkpoint: activate the double state too

Core A3 asks what changes when the double state also produces at activity a. Which end of the curve changes, and which state wins there?

Worked answer

The output becomes (R/K1+R2/(K1K2))/Z(R/K_1+R^2/(K_1K_2))/Z, one minus the empty fraction. The low end is unchanged, because G still wins below the first breakpoint. The high end changes. There CGRRC_{GRR} wins the promoter total, and it is now active, so the output saturates at a instead of falling as K2/RK_2/R. The window becomes a monotone saturation.

Run 2: a conformational switch

1 · Model. An allosteric protein with n equivalent sites takes two concerted conformations. MWC's historical letters label them R, for relaxed, which binds ligand tightly, and T, for tense, which binds it weakly. Lecture 7 called them active and inactive. Let L be the free ligand, KRK_R and KTK_T the site dissociation constants of the two conformations, and Λ the ratio of unliganded T to unliganded R. The state weights sum to

Z(L)=(1+LKR)n+Λ(1+LKT)n.Z(L)=\Bigl(1+\frac{L}{K_R}\Bigr)^n+\Lambda\Bigl(1+\frac{L}{K_T}\Bigr)^n.

The binomial expansion of each power counts the occupancy states of one conformation. The relaxed fraction is fR=(1+L/KR)n/Zf_R=(1+L/K_R)^n/Z. The mean number of bound ligands per protein is mˉ=L dlog⁡Z/dL\bar m=L\,d\log Z/dL. These are different readouts of one ensemble, and neither gives a catalytic rate without the activities of the states.16

2 · Experiment. Sweep free ligand in reservoir, and read fRf_R. The illustrative values are Λ=1000\Lambda=1000, n=4n=4, KR=1K_R=1 and KT=100 μMK_T=100\,\mu\mathrm M.

3 · Candidates. The protein total has two pooled candidates, the relaxed and the tense ensembles. At leading order each factor 1+L/K1+L/K is replaced by its larger term, max⁡(1,L/K)\max(1,L/K). That costs at most a factor of two per site, so at most 2n=162^n=16 per ensemble.

4 · Regime sequence. The tense ensemble wins at low ligand, because its weight is Λ against 1. The relaxed ensemble's weight grows as (L/KR)n(L/K_R)^n once L>KRL>K_R, while the tense weight stays near Λ below KTK_T. The relaxed ensemble therefore takes over at L⋆=KRΛ1/n=5.62 μML^\star=K_R\Lambda^{1/n}=5.62\,\mu\mathrm M, which lies below KTK_T as the step assumed.

29Negative cooperativity makes a buffer and a threshold

A two-site receptor separates binding cooperativity from response sharpness. With negative cooperativity, the singly occupied state absorbs the first ligand, and a threshold appears in total ligand. The pipeline shows where the threshold sits and why it needs finite supply.

1 · Model. Let qRq_R be the receptor total, L the free ligand, and K1K_1, K2K_2 the microscopic dissociation constants of the first and second occupation. The two singly occupied states are equivalent, so their pooled weight carries a factor of two:

w0=1,w1=2LK1,w2=L2K1K2,Z=w0+w1+w2,pi=wiZ.w_0=1,\qquad w_1=\frac{2L}{K_1},\qquad w_2=\frac{L^2}{K_1K_2},\qquad Z=w_0+w_1+w_2,\qquad p_i=\frac{w_i}{Z}.

Here pip_i is the fraction of receptors with i ligands, so CRL=qRp1C_{RL}=q_Rp_1 and CRL2=qRp2C_{RL_2}=q_Rp_2. The cooperativity is c=K1/K2c=K_1/K_2. Negative cooperativity means c<1c<1: the first ligand binds more readily than the second. Only the doubly occupied receptor is active, so the output is p2p_2. The ligand total closes the model:

qL=L+qR (p1+2p2).q_L=L+q_R\,(p_1+2p_2).

2 · Experiment. Sweep qLq_L at qR=1 μMq_R=1\,\mu\mathrm M, and read p2p_2. The illustrative affinities are (K1,K2)=(10−4,10−2) μM(K_1,K_2)=(10^{-4},10^{-2})\,\mu\mathrm M, so c=0.01c=0.01.

3 · Candidates. Both totals can change winner. The receptor total has candidates R, CRLC_{RL} and CRL2C_{RL_2}. The ligand total has candidates L, CRLC_{RL} and 2CRL22C_{RL_2}. A regime is named by the winners of (qR,qL)(q_R,q_L).

4 · Regime sequence. The path starts in (R,CRL)(R,C_{RL}): each ligand fills a first site. The binding relations then give L≈K1qL/(2qR)L\approx K_1q_L/(2q_R) and CRL2≈(c/4) qL2/qRC_{RL_2}\approx(c/4)\,q_L^2/q_R. The check CRL<RC_{RL}<R fails at qL=qRq_L=q_R, where CRLC_{RL} wins both totals, a singular ray. Past it the path is in (CRL,CRL2)(C_{RL},C_{RL_2}). A second singular ray at qL=2qRq_L=2q_R hands both totals to CRL2C_{RL_2}, and the path ends in (CRL2,L)(C_{RL_2},L).

The two rays carry balances, and with tight binding they hold across the whole middle interval. Subtracting totals cancels the complex that wins both:

qL−qR=L+CRL2−R,qL−2qR=L−CRL−2R.q_L-q_R=L+C_{RL_2}-R,\qquad q_L-2q_R=L-C_{RL}-2R.

Between the rays the free pools L and R are small, so the first balance gives p2≈qL/qR−1p_2\approx q_L/q_R-1. This is sharper than the regular law qL/(2qR)q_L/(2q_R), which holds only within its factor of two.

The table shows a buffer and then a threshold. With c=0.01c=0.01 the singly occupied state soaks up the first qRq_R of ligand and produces nothing. Output then rises along the ramp qL/qR−1q_L/q_R-1. With positive cooperativity, c=100c=100, the singly occupied state never wins, and the output rises from the start with no threshold. Finite affinity rounds the corners.

Ha and Ferrell tested the effect with DNA oligonucleotides. Their receptor strand bound two distinct ligand strands, and overlapping, separated or adjacent binding sequences changed the cooperativity. They measured the doubly bound product while varying the supplied ligands. The symmetric identical-ligand calculation above is their conceptual model. It is not a claim that their assay used identical ligands.17

The activity assignment is essential. If each bound ligand contributes independently, the output is proportional to p1+2p2p_1+2p_2, and the singly occupied receptors already produce half the full output. The buffering interval then vanishes in the tight limit. Negative cooperativity alone does not make a sharp regulatory response.

Read cooperativity from which occupied state wins, and read sharpness from the chosen activity and the ligand supply.

Two conformations with the same composition test the whole construction. The pipeline runs on an effective pair, and its table shows which parameters a bulk response can identify.

31Series binding tunes amplitude or threshold

A series architecture uses the first complex as the second binding partner. The downstream complex then enters the upstream totals, so the exact problem is coupled. The pipeline shows two hierarchies, one that tunes the output amplitude and one that tunes the input threshold.

1 · Model. Ligand L binds receptor R, and the complex binds a partner P:

L+R⇌k1,−k1,+CLR,CLR+P⇌k2,−k2,+CLRP.L+R\xrightleftharpoons[k_{1,-}]{k_{1,+}}C_{LR},\qquad C_{LR}+P\xrightleftharpoons[k_{2,-}]{k_{2,+}}C_{LRP}.

The dissociation constants are K1=k1,−/k1,+K_1=k_{1,-}/k_{1,+} and K2=k2,−/k2,+K_2=k_{2,-}/k_{2,+}. The active output is CLRPC_{LRP}. The totals are

qL=L+CLR+CLRP,qR=R+CLR+CLRP,qP=P+CLRP.q_L=L+C_{LR}+C_{LRP},\qquad q_R=R+C_{LR}+C_{LRP},\qquad q_P=P+C_{LRP}.

One scalar solve gives the exact state. Let B=CLR+CLRPB=C_{LR}+C_{LRP} be the ligand-bound receptor. Then CLR=(qL−B)(qR−B)/K1C_{LR}=(q_L-B)(q_R-B)/K_1 and CLRP=qPCLR/(K2+CLR)C_{LRP}=q_PC_{LR}/(K_2+C_{LR}), so B is the root of

F(B)=B−CLR(B)−qP CLR(B)K2+CLR(B)=0,0≤B≤min⁡(qL,qR).F(B)=B-C_{LR}(B)-\frac{q_P\,C_{LR}(B)}{K_2+C_{LR}(B)}=0,\qquad 0\le B\le\min(q_L,q_R).

On that interval CLR(B)C_{LR}(B) decreases, so F increases. F is nonpositive at the left end and nonnegative at the right end. Bisection therefore finds the unique physical state, with no reservoir assumption.

The downstream partner changes the upstream occupancy. Binding P lowers the free binary complex needed to hold a given B, so it draws more ligand and receptor into the bound population. Adding P can raise the first layer's occupancy with every binding constant fixed.

2 · Experiment. Sweep qLq_L, and read CLRPC_{LRP}. A regime is named by the winners of (qL,qR,qP)(q_L,q_R,q_P).

Here the receptor sets the threshold. Lowering the receptor total raises KeffK_{\mathrm{eff}}, so it can suppress activity without removing any ligand. The exact values follow the hyperbola qL/(Keff+qL)q_L/(K_{\mathrm{eff}}+q_L) to within one percent across the tested range.

Direct binding is the comparison. If L bound P directly, with dissociation constant KLPK_{LP} and qP≪KLPq_P\ll K_{LP}, the path would run from (L,P)(L,P) into (L,CLP)(L,C_{LP}) at qL=KLPq_L=K_{LP}. The series architecture adds one control knob in each hierarchy. The amplitude hierarchy adds the receptor factor to the plateau, and the threshold hierarchy adds it to the breakpoint. Each holds only under its own settling conditions, and the exact root covers the transitions between them.

Keep every downstream complex in the upstream totals, settle the totals the hierarchy allows, and read from the table which knob sets the amplitude and which sets the threshold.

32A modification cycle switches where both enzymes saturate

A modification cycle is the classic source of zero-order ultrasensitivity. The pipeline shows that its switch is a singular regime of the two enzyme totals. The finite model then proves separately that the steady state is unique and stable.

1 · Model. Enzyme E binds the unmodified target X with dissociation constant KEK_E, and enzyme F binds the modified target Y with KFK_F. Catalysis is composite at this resolution: CEX⇝E+YC_{EX}\rightsquigarrow E+Y with rate law kECEXk_EC_{EX}, and CFY⇝F+XC_{FY}\rightsquigarrow F+X with rate law kFCFYk_FC_{FY}. For a phosphorylation cycle these laws assume maintained co-substrates and negligible reverse activities. Binding conserves qEq_E, qFq_F, qX=X+CEXq_X=X+C_{EX} and qY=Y+CFYq_Y=Y+C_{FY}. Catalysis conserves the target total qtarget=qX+qYq_{\mathrm{target}}=q_X+q_Y.

The slow dynamics reduce to one equation. Write C(q1,q2,K)C(q_1,q_2,K) for the exact complex of one pair with totals q1q_1, q2q_2 and dissociation constant K, the root of §10:

C(q1,q2,K)=2q1q2T+T2−4q1q2,T=q1+q2+K.C(q_1,q_2,K)=\frac{2q_1q_2}{T+\sqrt{T^2-4q_1q_2}},\qquad T=q_1+q_2+K.

Then the modified total obeys

q˙Y=f(qY)=kE C(qE, qtarget−qY, KE)−kF C(qF, qY, KF).\dot q_Y=f(q_Y)=k_E\,C(q_E,\,q_{\mathrm{target}}-q_Y,\,K_E)-k_F\,C(q_F,\,q_Y,\,K_F).

The pair's complex increases with either total, because both of its gains are positive (§14). So f′(qY)<0f'(q_Y)<0 on the interior. Also f(0)>0f(0)>0 and f(qtarget)<0f(q_{\mathrm{target}})<0. The cycle therefore has exactly one steady state, and it is stable. A scalar root between zero and the target total computes it.

2 · Experiment. Vary the capacity ratio r=VE/VFr=V_E/V_F, with capacities VE=kEqEV_E=k_Eq_E and VF=kFqFV_F=k_Fq_F, and read the modified fraction y=qY/qtargety=q_Y/q_{\mathrm{target}}. Take trace enzymes, so complexes are negligible in the target totals, and write KˉE=KE/qtarget\bar K_E=K_E/q_{\mathrm{target}} and KˉF=KF/qtarget\bar K_F=K_F/q_{\mathrm{target}}. The steady balance VECEX/qE=VFCFY/qFV_EC_{EX}/q_E=V_FC_{FY}/q_F becomes

r 1−yKˉE+1−y=yKˉF+y⟺r=1+KˉE/(1−y)1+KˉF/y.r\,\frac{1-y}{\bar K_E+1-y}=\frac{y}{\bar K_F+y}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r=\frac{1+\bar K_E/(1-y)}{1+\bar K_F/y}.

The second form is exact, and each factor is an enzyme total over its complex. In trace, E/CEX=KE/X=KˉE/(1−y)E/C_{EX}=K_E/X=\bar K_E/(1-y), so the numerator is qE/CEXq_E/C_{EX}. Likewise the denominator is qF/CFYq_F/C_{FY}.

3 · Candidates. The target totals are settled, since the enzymes are in trace. The enzyme totals change winner. E's candidates are E and CEXC_{EX}, and CEXC_{EX} wins when KˉE<1−y\bar K_E<1-y. F's candidates are F and CFYC_{FY}, and CFYC_{FY} wins when KˉF<y\bar K_F<y. A regime is named by the winners of (qE,qF)(q_E,q_F).

4 · Regime sequence. Keeping the larger term of each factor gives the regimes. With KˉE,KˉF≪1\bar K_E,\bar K_F\ll1, the path runs from (CEX,F)(C_{EX},F), where r≈y/KˉFr\approx y/\bar K_F, into (CEX,CFY)(C_{EX},C_{FY}), where both factors are near one and r≈1r\approx1. It ends in (E,CFY)(E,C_{FY}), where r≈KˉE/(1−y)r\approx\bar K_E/(1-y). The middle regime is singular. Its leading-order law fixes r rather than y, so y jumps from about KˉF\bar K_F to about 1−KˉE1-\bar K_E across r=1r=1. The exact form above is the balance that places y inside the jump.

Prove uniqueness from the monotone pair complex, and read the switch from the regime where both enzyme totals are won by their complexes.

33The pipeline carries over to a new system

A new binding-catalysis system goes through the same three tools in a fixed order. Each tool has a check that the examples of this page have exercised.

Tool 1 builds the model. State the intervention and the readout first. List the molecular states, count their constituents into L, and check that the totals are complete (§1, §4). Assign one affinity per complex, with units, and one activity per state (§5, §16). Solve the positive allocation before simplifying anything (§6, §8).

Tool 2 maps the regimes. For each total, list its candidates and select, solve and check (§11). Keep the exact solve available at every boundary, and use the ray's balance wherever a singular crossing or a small difference carries the output (§13).

Tool 3 reads responses. Run the five steps of §15 along the path of the experiment, and end in a regime-sequence table with exact values beside the laws. Then test the dynamical closure on its own terms. Affinity data fix the allocation but not the relaxation, so compare clocks (§2) and check the reduced model against the resolved one on the output it must predict (§24). The extension runs the same three tools on a transporter that carries a physical current.

Transfer exercise with answer

In the conformational example of §30, suppose both bound states produce, at frequencies kocatk_{\mathrm o}^{\mathrm{cat}} and kccatk_{\mathrm c}^{\mathrm{cat}}. What changes in the pooled model and in its regime table?

Worked answer

The equilibrium inventory and Keff=Ko/(1+ρ)K_{\mathrm{eff}}=K_{\mathrm o}/(1+\rho) are unchanged. The effective activity becomes the population-weighted average

keff=kocat+ρ kccat1+ρ.k_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{k_{\mathrm o}^{\mathrm{cat}}+\rho\,k_{\mathrm c}^{\mathrm{cat}}}{1+\rho}.

The regime table keeps its breakpoint at qS=Keffq_S=K_{\mathrm{eff}}, and both pieces take the new keffk_{\mathrm{eff}}. If the two frequencies match, moving bound enzyme between conformations changes no activity per bound enzyme. Changing the conformational weight can still move the breakpoint through KeffK_{\mathrm{eff}}.

Build, map and read a new model in separate steps, and tie every approximation to the output it must predict.
